clue.text: Team players, catcalled, getting led off ground

indicators.note: something led off is walked away from where it was standing, so the letters it names leave the rest behind
ground is the past tense of grind, and anything put through a mill comes out in a different arrangement

parts.note: seven letters of fodder, taken as they stand
CATCALLED with LED taken off it, leaving six more letters of fodder

explanation.surface: Supporters jeer while a player is walked off the pitch.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Ground' closes the clue where a football ground would, and it is the milling instruction instead. 'Led off' is not a sending-off either: it names three letters to drop.
explanation.definitionFit: Crystal Palace is a football club in south London, so 'team' names it as plainly as a fixture list does.

clue.text: Mars communist plot–extremist gutted

parts.note: a red is a communist, after the colour of the flag
a plot is a plan, a scheme worked out in advance

indicators.note: to gut something is to take its insides out, which leaves only the letters on the outside

parts.note: the outside letters of ExtremisT

explanation.surface: A communist conspiracy with its most extreme members cut out of it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Mars' sits at the front, where a capital letter proves nothing, so it reads as the verb that spoils things rather than the planet. 'Gutted' is a standard request for a word's outside only.
explanation.definitionFit: Mars looks rust-coloured through a telescope because of the iron oxide on it, and 'the red planet' is the name that stuck.

clue.text: Frivolous cunning stopped by girl off and on

indicators.note: a gap stopped by a plug has the plug inside it, so the second piece sits within the first

parts.note: cunning means sly

indicators.note: switching off and on in turn means taking every other letter of the word

parts.note: the second and fourth letters of girl

explanation.surface: A sly scheme is foiled by a girl who keeps coming and going.
explanation.walkthrough: 'girl off and on' is not a fickle girlfriend: like a light switched off, on, off, on, it keeps only the second and fourth letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Silly and frivolous both describe behaviour lacking seriousness or good sense.

clue.text: Publicity staff in trouble for one month

indicators.note: one thing described as in another sits inside it, letters and all

parts.note: to ail somebody is to trouble them
pr = public relations, the department that handles publicity

explanation.surface: The press office endures four weeks of bad news.
explanation.walkthrough: 'For one' marks what follows as a class rather than a synonym, which is how a single example can be the definition. 'Trouble' is the verb here, not the noun the surface offers.
explanation.definitionFit: April is one of the twelve months, and 'for one' is the setter admitting that the definition names the class.

clue.text: What, when bad, could offer poor signs?

definitions.text: What, when bad, could offer poor signs?

indicators.note: something gone bad has gone wrong, and letters gone wrong are letters no longer in the order given

parts.note: the nine letters of fodder

explanation.surface: A question about the thing that, once it turns bad, starts showing poor indications.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue defines and builds at once, so 'bad' has two jobs: it belongs to the sense being described and it is the instruction to shuffle.
explanation.definitionFit: A prognosis is a doctor's forecast of how an illness will go, so a bad one is exactly a set of poor signs.

clue.text: Upset friend skips erotic performances

indicators.note: in a down clue, upset means turned upside down, so the word reads from bottom to top

parts.note: a pal is a friend
skips as a verb means dances lightly

explanation.surface: An upset friend storms out, skipping the erotic shows.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Upset' turns PAL upside down in this down clue, giving LAP; 'skips' is a verb here, not someone missing something.
explanation.definitionFit: Lap dances are strip-club routines performed close to, or on the lap of, a seated customer.

clue.text: Box upper section of body

definitions.meaning: a stout lidded box for blankets, tools or treasure
the front of the trunk, between neck and abdomen

explanation.surface: An instruction to punch somebody in the upper body.
explanation.walkthrough: Read as a sentence it tells you to hit a man in the ribs, and that verb reading is the whole disguise. Read as a clue it is two nouns laid side by side with no comma between them.
explanation.definitionFit: A chest is both a lidded storage box and the front of the body above the waist, two senses of one word.

clue.text: Bright and vigorous cook going around Asia dashes about

indicators.note: one thing going around another encloses it, so the second piece sits inside the first

parts.note: to fry is to cook

indicators.note: about here means all over the place, so the letters are scattered into a new order

explanation.surface: A chef rushes around Asia, dashing hither and thither.
explanation.walkthrough: 'dashes' looks like part of the frantic chef's travels, but it is just letters for the anagram, alongside ASIA; 'about' scrambles the pair.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom describes someone looking fresh, lively and full of energy, like a newly opened flower.

clue.text: Disrespect pro, shattering team spirit

indicators.note: a shattered thing lies in pieces, and pieces can be picked up in any order at all

parts.note: the thirteen letters of fodder

explanation.surface: Insulting a professional wrecks the mood of the whole side.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface says what the answer denies, since disrespecting a teammate really does shatter the thing being defined. The phrase is French taken whole, and it keeps its French spelling.
explanation.definitionFit: Esprit de corps is the shared pride and loyalty that binds a group, which plain English calls team spirit.

clue.text: Comic villain, one poking holes?

definitions.meaning: the Batman adversary who leaves puzzles behind at his crimes
to riddle a thing is to pierce it all over, so the agent noun follows

explanation.surface: A cartoon bad guy who goes about punching holes in things.
explanation.walkthrough: The second sense is the older one: a riddle is a coarse sieve, and to riddle something is to leave it full of holes. Both halves are nouns, which is the join a double definition needs.
explanation.definitionFit: The Riddler is the puzzle-setting villain of the Batman comics, and a riddler is separately anyone who riddles a thing with holes.

clue.text: Shore up tipsy old poet and musician

indicators.note: somebody tipsy is unsteady on their feet, and letters in that state will not stand where they were put

parts.note: the seven letters of fodder

explanation.surface: Propping up an unsteady old poet and musician.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Shore up' looks like the verb of the sentence, the thing being done to the drunk, and it is the fodder. 'Tipsy' reads as description of him and is the instruction.
explanation.definitionFit: In Greek myth Orpheus was the supreme poet and lyre-player, whose music moved rocks and charmed the dead.

clue.text: Small trifle spread out

parts.note: s = small, the clothes-label abbreviation
to trifle with something is to play with it

explanation.surface: A modest pudding laid out along the table.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Trifle' is the verb meaning to dally, not the sponge and custard the surface serves, and 'spread out' is the definition rather than more of the table setting.
explanation.definitionFit: To splay is to spread apart, the way fingers or the legs of a tripod do.

clue.text: Earl animatedly welcomes northern actors in royal house

indicators.note: a host who welcomes guests takes them in, so the second piece goes inside the first
animatedly means in a lively, jumbled way, so the letters move around

parts.note: the cast is the set of actors in a play

explanation.surface: A lively aristocrat greets a troupe of northern players at a royal palace.
explanation.walkthrough: The Earl looks like a title for the royal house, but it is only the anagram fodder; the scrambled letters split around the welcomed group.
explanation.definitionFit: The House of Lancaster was an English royal dynasty that held the throne during the Wars of the Roses.

clue.text: Scrap book, with second article removed

indicators.note: removed means taken away, so this piece is dropped from the word

parts.note: an annual is a book published yearly
A is the indefinite article; it is the second of the word's two that goes

explanation.surface: Throw out a book after a second article is taken out.
explanation.walkthrough: 'removed' drops an A from ANNUAL. An annual here is a yearly book, such as a children's comic collection; take away its second A.
explanation.definitionFit: To annul something is to cancel it formally, as you might scrap a plan or a marriage.

clue.text: Painting captures headland

parts.note: to land a fish or a contract is to capture it
a cape is a headland running out into the sea

explanation.surface: A picture catching a headland on canvas.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Captures' sits exactly where a container instruction would sit and is a plain synonym instead, since nothing in this clue goes inside anything. Three words, and two of them are wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: A landscape is a painting of open country, the genre taking its name from what it shows.

clue.text: Master of Arts thus runs away from Saviour, one who embraces suffering

parts.note: the initials of the degree
so = thus, therefore
CHRIST losing R, the cricket scorer's letter for runs

explanation.surface: An arts graduate accordingly bolts away from the Saviour.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Runs' is the scorecard's R waiting to be taken out, not a verb of fleeing, and that one word is what lets the whole surface read as an escape.
explanation.definitionFit: A masochist takes pleasure in pain, so the definition describes the taste rather than offering a synonym.

clue.text: Young person is able to head off southern islanders

parts.note: a minor is somebody under the age of majority
can = is able to

indicators.note: the head of a word is the letter it begins with, and here that letter comes off to be used on its own

parts.note: the head of Southern, detached

explanation.surface: A youngster manages to fend off some islanders from the south.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Head off' looks like fending something away and asks instead for a first letter to be detached. The definition is the final word on its own, which is as little as a clue can give you.
explanation.definitionFit: Minorca, the Balearic island east of Majorca, has Minorcans living on it — the English spelling of Menorca keeps the I.

clue.text: Chuck following one to north London borough

indicators.note: a piece that follows another is set down after it, so the throwing word comes second

parts.note: i = one, the Roman numeral
to chuck something is to sling it
the word is spelt out for its own two letters
n = north, the standard abbreviation

explanation.surface: A throw aimed after somebody on the road to a borough in north London.
explanation.walkthrough: 'North London' is how the surface wants to be read, and the split falls between them: the N is wordplay and London alone is definition. 'To' is spelt out rather than translated.
explanation.definitionFit: Islington is one of the thirty-two London boroughs, covering Angel and Highbury just north of the City.

clue.text: Roman emperor into Annus Horribilis?

indicators.note: the Latin for horrible, and a word in a horrible state is one with its letters in disarray

parts.note: the nine letters of fodder, the preposition included

explanation.surface: A Roman emperor dropped into a truly dreadful year.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Annus horribilis' is the Queen's own phrase for her dreadful 1992, and the italics flag it as Latin. 'Into' poses as the word joining two halves of a clue, and its four letters are needed.
explanation.definitionFit: Antoninus Pius ruled Rome from 138 to 161, and the name was carried by several later emperors as well.

clue.text: Victor interrupts only what you're now trying to do?

definitions.text: what you're now trying to do?

indicators.note: to interrupt is to cut in part of the way through, which is where the letter lands

parts.note: sole = only, the single one
v for Victor in the radio alphabet

explanation.surface: A man called Victor butts in on the one job you have in hand.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition points at the reader rather than at anything in the world, a wink setters allow themselves about once a puzzle. Victor is the radio alphabet's name for a letter, not a winner.
explanation.definitionFit: Working a clue out is solving it, so the definition simply describes what the reader is doing at that moment.

clue.text: Dicky ran castle of forebears

indicators.note: dicky is British for shaky or unsound — a dicky knee, a dicky heart — and nothing unsound holds its shape

parts.note: the nine letters of fodder

explanation.surface: A man called Dicky who used to run a castle.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Dicky' passes for a name standing in front of a verb, helped by the capital that begins every clue and proves nothing. In British use it means unsound or unreliable.
explanation.definitionFit: Ancestral means belonging to one's forebears, as an ancestral home or an ancestral right does.

clue.text: Company adopts radical belief

indicators.note: a family that adopts takes somebody into itself, so those letters go inside

parts.note: co = company, as on a firm's letterhead
a red is a political radical of the left

explanation.surface: A firm takes on a left-winger.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Radical' is a noun here, and red has stood for that politics since long before the Russian revolution. The definition is the last word by itself.
explanation.definitionFit: A credo is a statement of belief — Latin for 'I believe', and the name of the creed sung at Mass.

clue.text: Fine cotton left on edges of inlays and lace

indicators.note: in a down clue, one piece on another sits above it, so the letter for left comes first
and simply joins the two words whose edges are taken, one after the other
the edges of a word are its first and last letters, taken here from both words that follow

parts.note: first and last letters of inlays
first and last letters of lace

explanation.surface: Delicate cotton laid along the borders of inlays and lacework.
explanation.walkthrough: 'edges of' applies to both inlays and lace, giving IS and LE; 'on' puts L above them in this down clue.
explanation.definitionFit: Lisle is a smooth, strong cotton thread, once common in stockings and gloves.

clue.text: Fruit that stuffs German goose

indicators.note: whatever stuffs a bird is packed away inside it, out of sight

parts.note: GerMAN GOose carries it across the gap between the words

explanation.surface: A fruit used as the stuffing for a goose from Germany.
explanation.walkthrough: The join between two words is the hardest hiding place to see, because the eye insists on reading whole words. 'Stuffs' is both the hiding instruction and part of the cookery.
explanation.definitionFit: A mango is the sweet tropical stone fruit, so 'fruit' names it as flatly as a greengrocer would.

clue.text: Leaders among men of letters analyse rates that may be capped

definitions.note: The definition describes rather than names: it is a relative clause standing in for the noun, and the setter is entitled to it because only one sort of thing is meant.

indicators.note: the leader of a word is the letter standing at its head, and the clue wants one from each word that follows

parts.note: the opening letters of Men Of Letters Analyse Rates

explanation.surface: Writers go through figures that might have a ceiling put on them.
explanation.walkthrough: Capped rates are the surface's business, a limit on what can be charged, while the capping meant is a dentist's. 'Men of letters' reads as one phrase for writers and is really five words in a row.
explanation.definitionFit: A damaged tooth is given a crown, commonly called a cap, and a molar is the back grinding tooth that most often needs one.

clue.text: Composer worked at Mensa

indicators.note: dough that is worked is kneaded into a new shape, and letters take the same treatment

parts.note: the seven letters of fodder

explanation.surface: A composer holds down a job at the high-IQ society.
explanation.walkthrough: Mensa is the society for people scoring in the top two per cent on an IQ test, which is what lets the clue pass as a sentence about a clever man. 'Worked' is the instruction.
explanation.definitionFit: Bedřich Smetana was the nineteenth-century Czech composer of Má vlast and The Bartered Bride.

clue.text: Separate tips of spark plugs illuminated

indicators.note: the tip of each word is its first letter

parts.note: the first letters of spark and plugs
illuminated means lit up

explanation.surface: An engine's spark plugs flash and light up separately.
explanation.walkthrough: 'tips of' gives SP from spark plugs; 'Separate' is a verb here, as couples do.
explanation.definitionFit: To split up is to separate, especially of a couple ending their relationship.

clue.text: Accessory that facilitates change of direction in estate?

definitions.text: Accessory that facilitates change of direction
definitions.meaning: on the surface this is any fitting that helps something take a new course, which is how the sentence asks to be read
an estate is also an estate car, and the question mark is the setter admitting that the accessory comes on every other model too

explanation.surface: A fitting that helps a landed estate change the direction it is going in.
explanation.walkthrough: Nothing here breaks into letters: no fodder, no indicator, no container. The lever is 'estate', which the surface wants as land and property and the setter means as a car with a long back.
explanation.definitionFit: Power steering uses the engine to turn the front wheels, so it is precisely the accessory that makes changing direction easy in a car.
